reviewed.by: Science&Faith batch (9 essays, 69 takeaways): apologia-argument SOUND (0 CRITICAL/MAJOR; 2 optional MINOR applied) + apologia-orthodoxy CLEAN (0 heresy/drift; 1 optional NOTE applied). Argument-specific rules held: kalam begins-to-exist, fine-tuning data-conceded/design-inferred (never 'scientists agree it's designed'), laws describe-not-prescribe, miracles possible-not-proven. Single-gate (Science&Faith).

batches.by: apologia-argument SOUND (0 CRITICAL/MAJOR; 2 MINOR + 2 POLISH applied) + apologia-orthodoxy CLEAN-after-fix (2 evil.html standalone-pull-quote lines fixed). Rules held: kalam begins-to-exist; morality duties-need-a-ground + 'atheists can be good'; evil = Plantinga consistency-not-proof + no tidy theodicy + redemptive anchor; contingency/Five Ways/ontological = philosophical terminus not the Nicene God.

bigbang.Stating the Argument Carefully: Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so it has a cause—not yet God.
bigbang.The Science Behind “The Universe Began”: Expansion, the CMB, and light-element ratios converge on a cosmic beginning—though not a proven first instant.
bigbang.From a Beginning to a Cause: A beginning points to a transcendent, immaterial, powerful cause—its personhood a further, contested inference.
bigbang.The Live Alternatives, Taken Seriously: Serious alternatives to a beginning exist, but each smuggles in a structured “something” or faces real pressure.
bigbang.Where the Debate Actually Stands: The hot Big Bang is undisputed; whether the past boundary is a true beginning remains contested.
bigbang.What This Does and Does Not Establish: It doesn't prove God, but overturns the old default of an eternal, self-existing universe—a beginning that cries out for a cause.

cosmic.Stating the Question Carefully: The physical data are conceded; that purpose best explains them is a contested inference, not proof.
cosmic.How the Argument Developed: Design reasoning runs from Aristotle to a modern cosmic version built on order, intelligibility, and entropy.
cosmic.The First Strand: An Improbably Ordered: The universe's low-entropy beginning is astonishingly special—the kind of order a purposing mind might supply.
cosmic.The Second Strand: A Universe That Can B: That the cosmos is intelligible to minds fits a rational Creator better than blind chance.
cosmic.The Third Strand: A Cosmos Built to Be D: Habitability seems to correlate with discoverability—suggestive of purpose, though this is the most contested strand.
cosmic.The Strongest Objections: Anthropic selection, the multiverse, and cosmic waste each strike real blows—but carry their own unpaid costs.
cosmic.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The physics is undisputed; its interpretation is genuinely split, and no view is cost-free.
cosmic.What It Does, and Does Not, Establish: At most it points to a rational mind behind the cosmos—defensible, but honestly resistible.

laws.Stating the Question Carefully: The metaphysical question—why any order exists—points, as best explanation and not proof, toward a Mind.
laws.What Philosophers Mean by “a Law of Natu: Laws may be mere descriptions or genuine governors; the deep puzzle of order survives either view.
laws.The Argument’s Long History: The very idea of universal law arose within a theistic frame and was later sharpened philosophically.
laws.Premise 1: The Cosmos Is Deeply, Intelli: Nature is uniformly, mathematically ordered and—strangely—intelligible to minds; this premise is barely disputed.
laws.The Contingency of the Particular Laws: The particular laws appear contingent—could have been otherwise—which invites, contestably, a demand for explanation.
laws.Premise 2: Why a Mind Explains This Bett: The theist argues a rational Mind is a better terminus for cosmic order than an unexplained brute fact—a comparative claim, not a proof.
laws.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Laws describe, not prescribe, so “who made them?” may be a category mistake; every worldview stops somewhere.
laws.The Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Car: Even granting laws are mere descriptions, why the cosmos is orderly at all still needs explaining.
laws.The Multiverse and the “Final Theory” Re: A multiverse only relocates the order, and a final theory still wouldn't breathe fire into equations.
laws.The Honest State of Scholarship: The metaphysics of laws is unsettled; the theistic reading is a respectable minority, not consensus.
laws.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: It doesn't prove God, but cosmic order is more at home with a Mind than without.

mathematics.Wigner Names the Puzzle: Wigner called mathematics' effectiveness in physics a mysterious gift with “no rational explanation.”
mathematics.The Argument, Stated Carefully: Math's uncanny fit with the world is some evidence—not proof—of a rational mind behind reality.
mathematics.The Evidence: When Pure Mathematics Arri: Pure mathematics repeatedly predicted unseen physical reality—the predictive cases are hardest to explain away.
mathematics.Four Philosophies of Mathematics—and Why: No philosophy of mathematics—Platonist, nominalist, fictionalist, or structuralist—dissolves the puzzle of its effectiveness.
mathematics.The Theistic Proposal: If reality flows from a rational Creator, its intelligibility and our grasp of it are expected, not lucky.
mathematics.The Strongest Objections—Stated at Full: The strongest objections cap or relocate the puzzle of mathematical effectiveness, but none pays it off.
mathematics.The Indispensability Debate, and an Hone: How real mathematics is remains disputed—and the argument is stronger the more real it is.
mathematics.The State of the Scholarship: The effectiveness is undisputed; its explanation is wide open, and the theistic reading is one serious option.
mathematics.What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Es: It doesn't prove God, but a world written in reason is more at home with a Mind.

originlife.What Abiogenesis Must Explain: Abiogenesis must explain metabolism, replication, and—deepest of all—the origin of specified biological information.
originlife.The Experimental Program, and Its Limits: Real experimental progress notwithstanding, no program has bridged chemistry to a coded, self-replicating cell.
originlife.The Design Inference from Information: Intelligence is the only known source of specified information, making design the best current explanation—defeasibly.
originlife.Steelmanning the Mainstream Program: The god-of-the-gaps charge, disputed probability numbers, and unknown early conditions are serious objections honestly conceded.
originlife.The State of the Scholarship: There's no consensus origin-of-life mechanism, but none is proven impossible; design remains a minority view.
originlife.What the Argument Does and Doesn’t Estab: It doesn't prove design, but shows life's information is a real mystery whose only known source is mind.

cambrian.What the “Explosion” Actually Is: Most major animal body plans appear in a geologically short Cambrian window—a real, agreed-upon event.
cambrian.Darwin’s Doubt—and Whose Doubt It Was: Darwin himself conceded the puzzle; Meyer reframes it as the origin of new biological information.
cambrian.The Case for the Premises, at Its Strong: The explosion is real and partly unexplained; the case leans on rare protein folds and rigid developmental networks.
cambrian.The Mainstream Reply, Stated Fairly and: Most biologists answer with a longer timeline, deeper divergences, patchy preservation, and rewiring of existing genes.
cambrian.Weighing the Exchange Honestly: Design fastens onto a real open problem, but its empirical premises are softer and more contested than its rhetoric.
cambrian.The Honest State of the Question: The data are agreed; the design inference is contested, not consensus, and rests on disputed estimates.
cambrian.Conclusion: What It Does and Does Not Sh: It doesn't refute evolution or prove design, but raises a serious challenge best held with humility.

privileged.Stating the Thesis Carefully: The conditions for life may also make the cosmos knowable—a checkable claim, with design a separate, contested inference.
privileged.How the Idea Developed: Building on the secular “Rare Earth” work, Gonzalez and Richards added that habitability also aids discovery.
privileged.Premise 1: Does the Correlation Hold?: The habitability–discoverability correlation is suggestive but under-tested—a pattern, not a demonstrated theorem.
privileged.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Critics answer with observer selection, cherry-picking, unfalsifiability, and the Copernican principle of mediocrity.
privileged.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: Selection can't explain the cosmos's surplus intelligibility, but the correlation stays under-quantified—a clue, not a proof.
privileged.The Honest State of the Debate: Habitability science is respectable; the measurability correlation isn't mainstream, and most astronomers reject it.
privileged.Conclusion: What the Thesis Does and Doe: It doesn't prove design, but the cosmos being knowable, not just livable, fits theism as a modest clue.

finetuning.The Numbers That Stopped the Physicists: The physical constants sit in eerily narrow life-permitting ranges—arithmetic that unsettled even hardened physicists.
finetuning.What Fine-Tuning Actually Means: Fine-tuning means the fundamental constants lie in ranges so slim small changes would forbid life's chemistry.
finetuning.Three Doors: Chance, Necessity, Design: Chance, necessity, or design; by the likelihood principle fine-tuning tilts toward design—confirmation, not proof.
finetuning.The Strongest Objections: The multiverse, the anthropic “puddle,” and the measure problem are the argument's strongest challenges.
finetuning.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The data are undisputed; the interpretation is contested, and design earns a seat among serious explanations.
finetuning.What It Does, and Does Not, Establish: It points at most to a fine-tuner, never “scientists agree it's designed”—defensible, but honestly resistible.

miracles.Stating the Question Carefully: Keep possibility (philosophy) apart from actuality (evidence); the a priori bar on miracles is what's contested.
miracles.What a Miracle Is—and Is Not: A miracle is a special act of God transcending nature—a coherent concept, even to atheists like Flew.
miracles.Descriptions, Not Prescriptions: Laws describe how things behave when nothing interferes; an agent introducing a new cause violates nothing.
miracles.The Closed Box and the Open One: Whether the universe is causally closed is a metaphysical assumption, not a scientific finding.
miracles.Spinoza: Miracles as an Absurdity: Spinoza's impossibility argument begs the question and works only given his pantheism, which no theist holds.
miracles.Hume: Miracles as Never Credible: Hume argued no testimony could ever make a miracle credible—a serious objection to weigh honestly, not to mock.
miracles.Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down: Hume fails three ways: rare events can be well-attested, “uniform experience” is circular, and his weighing is skewed.
miracles.The State of the Scholarship: The confident a priori dismissal has collapsed; the debate has moved to weighing evidence case by case.
miracles.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: This only unbars the door: miracles are possible and worth investigating, never that any actually occurred.

thomistic.The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's whole case hangs on the kind of causal series he means — misread it and you refute a phantom.
thomistic.The Five Ways in Brief: The Five Ways sketch five routes to God as the world's ultimate source; the First Way is the paradigm.
thomistic.The Single Most Important Point: The series is simultaneous and here-and-now, requiring a present sustainer, not a first event long ago.
thomistic.The Metaphysics Beneath the First Way: Change is a potential becoming actual, and only something purely actual can ground the chain.
thomistic.The Objections — Steelmanned: Aquinas never claimed everything has a cause; the inertia objection is the one demanding a real reply.
thomistic.The Honest State of the Scholarship: There is no consensus either way, but the lazy dismissals of the argument no longer survive.
thomistic.What the Five Ways Do and Do Not Establi: If sound, the Ways reach a sustaining first cause — not yet the good, personal, triune God.

kalam.A question that refuses to stay small: Either the universe is eternal or it began — and which it is changes everything.
kalam.The argument, stated with care: Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause.
kalam.Premise 1: out of nothing, nothing comes: Being does not arise from non-being; the quantum vacuum is something, not nothing.
kalam.Premise 2: the case for a beginning: Both philosophy and cosmology point to a beginning, though the science corroborates rather than proves it.
kalam.From a cause to a Creator: The cause must be spaceless, timeless, immaterial, powerful, and plausibly a personal mind.
kalam.The strongest objections, fairly stated: 'What caused God?' misreads premise 1, but critics like Morriston and Oppy keep the debate open.
kalam.The honest state of the debate: The argument stays live and contested; the step from cause to person is most disputed.
kalam.What Kalam does and does not establish: Kalam makes a serious case for a transcendent cause, not a proof of any particular God.

leibniz.The Most Persistent Question: The question 'why is there anything at all?' stands whether or not the universe began.
leibniz.The Argument, Stated Carefully: A contingent universe needs an explanation beyond itself: a necessary, transcendent being.
leibniz.The Strongest Objections: The deepest objections attack the Principle of Sufficient Reason and offer the cosmos as a brute stopping point.
leibniz.The Honest State of the Scholarship: Philosophers still divide over the PSR and whether the universe can simply be 'just there.'
leibniz.What It Does, and Doesn't, Establish: If sound, it reaches a necessary ground of being — one strand toward, not yet, the personal God.

beauty.The Datum: Beauty in Nature, Art, and Nu: Beauty in nature, art, and mathematics is a real datum any worldview must explain.
beauty.The Argument and Its History: Beauty fits more naturally with a Creator who is its source than with blind matter.
beauty.The Case at Its Strongest: The convergence of beauty, elegant laws, and minds that delight in them favors one Author.
beauty.The Objections, Steelmanned: Evolution, aesthetic subjectivism, and nature's ugliness each press hard against the argument.
beauty.Replies — and Honest Concessions: Real replies exist, but beauty's objectivity is contested and nature's ugliness blunts the argument's edge.
beauty.The State of Scholarship: Even its defenders treat beauty as one modest strand, not a stand-alone proof.
beauty.Conclusion: What It Does and Does Not Es: Beauty does not prove God, but theism explains it more gracefully than naturalism does.

consciousness.The Hard Problem: Why physical processes are accompanied by inner experience resists ordinary scientific reduction.
consciousness.The Argument Stated: Consciousness is more expected if reality is grounded in Mind than in blind matter.
consciousness.The Force of the Argument: Naturalism explains the mental by the non-mental — but consciousness is what will not reduce.
consciousness.Objections, Stated at Full Strength: Even if materialism fails, panpsychism and naturalistic dualism, not only God, remain live options.
consciousness.The State of the Scholarship: The hard problem is taken seriously, yet physicalism persists and this is no proof of God.
consciousness.Conclusion: What It Establishes, and Wha: Consciousness favors a mental ground over pure physicalism — a clue, not a proof.

desire.The argument stated: A longing nothing earthly satisfies is best explained, Lewis says, by our being made for more.
desire.The longing and its history: The restless longing Lewis called Joy runs from Augustine and Aquinas through Romanticism.
desire.Why the argument has force: Natural desires reliably track real objects, so a universal longing aimed at nothing would be strange.
desire.The objections, stated at full strength: Wanting something does not make it exist, and critics call the natural/artificial distinction rigged.
desire.Replying—while conceding what must be co: It is no proof; the case rests on the peculiar shape of a longing survival cannot fully explain.
desire.The state of the question: Philosophers treat the argument as serious but minor — a contributor, not a decisive proof.
desire.What it does, and does not, establish: It does not prove God, but argues our longing is as well explained by design as by mistake.

reason.The Argument Stated: If our beliefs are merely the products of non-rational causes, the naturalist has no reason to trust his own reasoning.
reason.A History of an Idea: From Balfour and Haldane to Lewis, thinkers pressed that naturalism undercuts trust in reason.
reason.Plantinga's Rigorous Cousin: Plantinga argues naturalism plus evolution gives us a defeater for trusting our own minds.
reason.The Strongest Objections: Anscombe's level distinction and the 'true beliefs aid survival' reply are the strongest challenges.
reason.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The argument is unresolved — a live problem for naturalism, not a settled refutation.
reason.What It Does — and Does Not — Establish: It is a problem for naturalism, not a proof of God — reason fits a rational source better.

religious.The claim, stated carefully: An apparent experience of God carries genuine, defeasible weight — not proof, but evidence.
religious.Two modern defenses: Swinburne and Alsto: Swinburne and Alston argue religious experience deserves the same default trust we give perception.
religious.The objections, taken at full strength: Neuroscience, conflicting religious claims, and Freud's projection are the serious objections — diversity the strongest.
religious.The honest state of the question: Experience cannot settle which God is real, but gives the experiencer genuine, non-dismissable warrant.

ontological.The Argument That Tries to Reach God by: The ontological argument tries to reach God from the bare concept of God alone.
ontological.Anselm's Original: Greatness That Cannot: Anselm argues the greatest conceivable being cannot coherently be thought of as failing to exist.
ontological.Descartes: Existence as a Perfection: Descartes treats existence as a perfection the supremely perfect being must possess.
ontological.The Modern Modal Version: Plantinga: If a maximally great being is even possible, Plantinga argues, it exists necessarily.
ontological.The Strongest Objections: Kant retired the older forms; the modal version stalls on whether God is even possible.
ontological.What Plantinga Actually Claimed: Plantinga claimed only that the argument shows theistic belief is rational, not that it proves God.
ontological.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The argument is valid; the whole debate now rests on the contested possibility premise.
ontological.Conclusion: What It Does and Doesn't Est: It does not prove God, but shows a maximally great being is either necessary or impossible.

moral.The Argument and Its History: If objective moral duties are real, they need a ground beyond human opinion.
moral.Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really W: That some acts are really wrong is a properly basic conviction shared even by secular realists.
moral.Premise 1: What Grounds the Moral Law?: The claim is not that atheists cannot be good, but that objective morality needs grounding in God's nature.
moral.The Euthyphro Dilemma: Goodness is neither arbitrary command nor a standard above God, but God's own necessary nature.
moral.The Strongest Objection: Wielenberg's Go: Wielenberg grounds morality in brute necessary facts; the theist replies duties must be owed to someone.
moral.The Darwinian Dilemma — Which Cuts Both: Evolutionary debunking of moral intuitions cuts against secular realism at least as hard as theism.
moral.What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Es: If sound, it reaches a good lawgiver — not the full Christian God — never impugning atheists' goodness.

evil.Stating the problem at its strongest: The problem comes in three forms — logical, evidential, and existential — of rising difficulty.
evil.The logical problem, and why most philos: Plantinga's defense shows God and evil can consistently coexist — not why evil exists, only that it can.
evil.The evidential problem: the genuinely ha: The hard version asks whether pointless suffering makes God unlikely; no reply is tidy or complete.
evil.The cross: not a theodicy but a presence: Christianity offers not a tidy explanation but a God who entered suffering and promises to defeat it.
evil.The critic's last word — and a reply: The skeptic's intuition retains real weight; the theist's reply is a defensible reframing that keeps faith reasonable, not a claimed victory.
evil.The honest state of the question: The logical problem failed and the evidential remains unresolved — but the grief no argument can relieve is met by the God who entered it.
